article_title: Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models
citation: Eric Isenberg, Bing-ru Teh, Elias Walsh. (2013). Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models. Working Paper 23, Chicago, IL: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers using elementary administrative data for value-added models should attend to teacher/student link accuracy before estimation
description: Because unconfirmed administrative data can link "about one in six teachers in these grades and subjects" to a subject they do not teach, researchers using value-added models with elementary school data should verify teacher/student links, for example through a roster confirmation process, before estimation. The paper motivates this by comparing confirmed and unconfirmed links in DC Public Schools data.
requirements: Access to a roster confirmation process or equivalent means for teachers to verify the subjects and students they taught
constraints: Mislinking arises specifically from departmentalization of instruction in math and reading/English language arts in grades 4 and 5
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of teacher effects in value-added models
examples: The working paper compares roster-confirmed teacher/student links to unconfirmed administrative links in DC Public Schools
key_sources: Eric Isenberg, Bing-ru Teh, Elias Walsh. (2013). Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models. Working Paper 23, Chicago, IL: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementary-school-data-issues-implications-for-research-using-valueadded-models

article_title: The (non)impact of differential test taker engagement on aggregated scores
citation: Steven Wise, James Soland, Yuanchao Bo. (2019). The (non)impact of differential test taker engagement on aggregated scores. International Journal of Testing 20 (1), 55-77. https://www.tandfonline.com/
title: Do not assume low-stakes aggregated school scores are invalid solely because of differential test-taker engagement; check whether disengagement effects cancel or dilute
description: The article argues that differential engagement on low-stakes tests does not necessarily invalidate aggregated school-level scores. In its PISA-Based Test for Schools data, school means were "highly stable due to two factors": dilution by engaged students and cancellation of positive and negative individual distortions. The principle directs measurement users to examine these mechanisms before discounting aggregated scores.
requirements: Evidence about the proportion of students exhibiting no non-effortful behavior and the direction of individual score distortions in the assessment of interest
constraints: The finding is specific to the computer-based version of the PISA-Based Test for Schools; the abstract notes disengagement is most prevalent with low-stakes tests
target_learners: K-12 students taking low-stakes school-level assessments
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of aggregated school-level achievement scores
examples: The study examined distortive effects of differential engagement on aggregated school-level scores using data from the computer-based version of the PISA-Based Test for Schools
key_sources: Steven Wise, James Soland, Yuanchao Bo. (2019). The (non)impact of differential test taker engagement on aggregated scores. International Journal of Testing 20 (1), 55-77. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-nonimpact-of-differential-test-taker-engagement-on-aggregated-scores/

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Verification and accountability practices requiring learners to demonstrate how GenAI-sourced claims were checked
description: Verification practices require learners to demonstrate how claims were checked, what sources were consulted, and how discrepancies or uncertainty were addressed. The paper positions verification as "an ethical responsibility inherent to academic work", operationalizing accountability: learners remain responsible for accuracy regardless of whether claims originated from GenAI. This makes integrity enacted through epistemic vigilance rather than presumed through trust in technological outputs.
requirements: Assessment must make verification an explicit component rather than treating GenAI inaccuracies as evidence of misconduct
constraints: Responds to the probabilistic nature of GenAI outputs, which may include fabricated citations or misleading summaries
target_learning_goals: critical information literacy and disciplinary accountability
examples: The paper connects such practices to emerging paired-component designs that verify learning outcomes in AI-vulnerable contexts
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Reshaping Undergraduate Computer Science Education in the Generative AI Era
citation: Reshaping Undergraduate Computer Science Education in the Generative AI Era. (2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07545
title: Verification spectrum: a graduate competency spanning informal code review and testing through static analysis and type-system-guided development to full formal verification
description: The verification spectrum is the whitepaper's articulation of verification as a durable graduate competency for the AI era, extending the CS2023 framework. In the faculty workshop's usage, "verification" in this context encompasses a spectrum of rigor: from informal code review and testing, through static analysis and type-system-guided development, to full formal verification using proof assistants. Humans act as a senior software engineer verifying AI-generated code, and the whitepaper argues this spectrum aligns with a three-level framework from the formal methods education literature that can be embedded in existing courses without additional curricular expansion.
requirements: Embedding verification thinking within existing courses without requiring additional curricular expansion, per the framework the whitepaper cites
constraints: The whitepaper notes neither workshop drew a clear distinction between informal and formal verification approaches, so the precise meaning of verification as a graduate competency remains underspecified
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students, particularly those verifying AI-generated code
target_learning_goals: specifying intended behaviour precisely and verifying that implementations conform to specifications
examples: Faculty workshop participants positioned verification as the crucial skill in which humans play the role of a senior software engineer overseeing AI models that act as junior engineers
key_sources: Reshaping Undergraduate Computer Science Education in the Generative AI Era. (2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07545

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model
citation: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707
title: Verification-centered Johnstone-3P architecture for GenAI in university chemistry education
description: The review proposes an explanatory architecture in which Johnstone's chemistry triplet (macroscopic, submicroscopic, symbolic domains, with representational translation as a cross-domain process rather than a fourth level) supplies a chemistry-specific epistemic test, and Biggs' Presage-Process-Product model supplies the pedagogical conditions. As the review states, "Johnstone’s triplet identifies the disciplinary location of this risk, while Biggs’ 3P model shows that outcomes depend on readiness, task design, policy, and assessment." Presage conditions shape learners' capacity to verify; process-level prompting, critique, and revision operate across the three domains; product outcomes must be demonstrated rather than assumed.
requirements: Learners must possess sufficient prior chemistry knowledge and representational competence to verify outputs, since students cannot verify what they do not understand
constraints: The review treats representational translation as a cross-domain reasoning process, not a fourth level of the triplet
The framework is developed for university chemistry, biochemistry, chemical engineering, and chemistry teacher education contexts
target_learning_goals: Coordinating macroscopic, submicroscopic, and symbolic reasoning
Chemical accuracy and representational fluency
Professional judgment and laboratory responsibility
examples: Figure 1 presents the hierarchy linking presage conditions, cross-domain verification processes, and demonstrated product outcomes
key_sources: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707

article_title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
citation: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698
title: VeriForge mixed-initiative writing system with proactive highlighting, dual-stream querying, Knowledge Canvas, and graph-based RAG
description: VeriForge is a mixed-initiative writing environment that divides cognitive labor so "the system assumes initiative over domain discovery while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis". Its front-end couples flow-aware proactive inline highlighting (fading in after a 5-second keystroke pause), a dual-stream query panel pairing conversational text with color-coded source-anchored Knowledge Cards, and a spatial Knowledge Canvas with gold nodes from highlights and silver nodes from queries connected by AI Auto-Reasoned edges. A graph-based RAG back-end in Neo4j binds provenance to every node at ingestion time, so "every retrieved fact remains traceable to its exact source passage".
requirements: Authors upload curated domain source texts, which the system ingests into a domain knowledge graph, typically requiring 5 to 10 minutes per book
constraints: Evaluated in 30-minute cold-start sessions on historical martial-arts writing domains; the authors state this bounds where VeriForge has been shown to work, not where the problem exists
target_learners: Fiction writers venturing into unfamiliar domains, including hobbyists and online novelists
target_learning_goals: Discovering and integrating unfamiliar domain knowledge into narrative prose with verisimilitude
examples: In the system walkthrough, novelist Marie drafts a medieval duel; the system highlights longsword after a 5-second keystroke pause, and a Knowledge Card separates an AI-generated description from a quoted source passage
key_sources: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698

article_title: How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis
citation: Sungeun An, Jennifer Hammock, Ashok Goel. (2025). How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00506-5
title: VERA (Virtual Experimentation Research Assistant) ecological modeling tool
description: VERA is a publicly available online tool for ecological modeling, accessible via the Smithsonian's Encyclopedia of Life site, that "supports conceptual modeling, agent-based simulations, and hypothesis-driven experiments". It uses the Component-Mechanism-Phenomenon (CMP) language grounded in biodiversity knowledge bases, scaffolds parameter setting with Encyclopedia of Life trait data, and automatically generates NetLogo agent-based simulations from conceptual models via an AI compiler, supporting model-simulate-refine loops. Its detailed interaction logging (17 distinct actions, clickstream data, XML models) enables fine-grained learning analytics research.
requirements: Access to the Encyclopedia of Life biodiversity knowledge base for parameter scaffolding
interaction logging infrastructure to capture modeling actions
constraints: The article states demographic data such as grade level or scores are not collected, as with other open online platforms
target_learning_goals: ecological conceptual modeling
hypothesis-driven experimentation
examples: A study on college students demonstrated that use of VERA improves content knowledge of ecological systems (An et al., 2018), as cited by the article
key_sources: Sungeun An, Jennifer Hammock, Ashok Goel. (2025). How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00506-5

article_title: Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults
citation: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9
title: Vestibular stimulation as a mediator of exercise effects on memory and spatial cognition
description: The article proposes that "an increased stimulation of the vestibular system during self-motion might be an essential mediator between physical exercise and cognitive functioning". Vestibular nuclei connect to the cerebellum, hippocampus and parietal cortices supporting spatial functions and memory; the authors speculate that balance training induces hippocampal and parietal changes via direct vestibular pathways. This account explains why cognitive gains occurred without cardiorespiratory fitness improvement.
requirements: Training must impose high demands on the vestibular system, e.g. reactive postural adjustments on varying surfaces
constraints: The vestibular mechanism is explicitly speculative: the authors write it "might be speculated" and that whether sub-processes or multisensory integration is essential "must be addressed in future studies"
target_learning_goals: memory
spatial cognition
examples: The balance circuit training used eight stations with tasks like single-leg stance while pulled by an elastic strap, designed to force permanent re-stabilization
key_sources: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9

article_title: Relationship between cognitive function and prevalence of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation in adolescents
citation: Mizuno K, Tanaka M, Fukuda S, Imai-Matsumura K, Watanabe Y. (2011). Relationship between cognitive function and prevalence of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation in adolescents. Behavioral and Brain Functions 7:4. https://doi.org/10.1186/1744-9081-7-4
title: Use verbal memory tests (digit span forward and kana pick-out) to objectively evaluate the extent of decreased intrinsic academic motivation in junior high students
description: The article recommends measuring capacity for verbal memory as an objective indicator of decreased intrinsic academic motivation in early adolescence. It states that "measurement of capacity for verbal memory is useful for objectively evaluating the extent of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation", naming the digit span forward test and kana pick-out test as appropriate for this age group. This rests on the cross-sectional associations reported for junior high students.
requirements: Applies to junior high school students (7th-9th grade); the associations were not found in elementary students.
constraints: Cross-sectional findings do not establish cause-and-effect; the study had a limited number of participants and did not measure socioeconomic or psychological status or intelligence quotient.
target_learning_goals: Early detection of decline in intrinsic academic motivation
examples: The study administered the digit span forward test and kana pick-out test alongside a 30-item intrinsic academic motivation questionnaire to students in grades 4-9 in Hyogo Prefecture, Japan.
key_sources: Mizuno K, Tanaka M, Fukuda S, Imai-Matsumura K, Watanabe Y. (2011). Relationship between cognitive function and prevalence of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation in adolescents. Behavioral and Brain Functions 7:4. https://doi.org/10.1186/1744-9081-7-4

article_title: Enhanced verbal abilities in the congenitally blind
citation: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/
title: Congenital blindness confers a specific verbal advantage rather than a general memory enhancement
description: The article proposes that congenital blindness produces superiority specifically in verbal abilities rather than a domain-general enhancement of memory. This account explains why blind participants outperformed sighted controls on verbal memory, verbal fluency, and verbal working memory while performing equally on spatial memory and spatial imagery. The authors suggest "congenital blindness induces stronger reliance on verbal information, and that such reliance leads to better verbal memory, and potentially other verbal skills, through practice."
requirements: Requires congenital blindness from birth, as the account rests on lifelong adaptation to the absence of visual input
constraints: The mechanism by which the superiority of verbal abilities occurs is currently unknown, per the authors
The study tested a limited range of tasks, so whether superiority extends across all language skills remains open
target_learning_goals: Verbal memory and verbal skill development
examples: Blind participants outperformed sighted controls on all verbal tasks but not on spatial tasks in the same participants
key_sources: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/

article_title: Early language and executive skills predict variations in number and arithmetic skills in children at family-risk of dyslexia and typically developing controls
citation: Moll K., Snowling M. J., Göbel S. M., Hulme C. (2015). Early language and executive skills predict variations in number and arithmetic skills in children at family-risk of dyslexia and typically developing controls. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.03.004
title: Verbal number skills as the mediating pathway from early language and executive skills to formal arithmetic
description: The article proposes a developmental pathway in which language and executive skills at 3–4 years constrain children's ability to learn to count and to match Arabic numerals to verbal labels one year later, and these exact verbal number skills in turn support formal arithmetic. As the authors conclude, "Language and executive skills at 3–4 years of age constrain the ability to learn to count and to match Arabic numerals to their verbal labels one year later and exert an indirect influence on arithmetic ability via these more proximal domain-specific precursors." This account explains why problems in early language development may explain the comorbidity between reading and mathematics disorder.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment beginning before formal education to trace causal influences
constraints: Non-verbal number skills such as estimation or magnitude comparison were not measured, so the theory concerns verbal number skills specifically
target_learning_goals: counting
number knowledge
arithmetic development
examples: The multi-group path model fitting this pathway to 169 children showed complete mediation with excellent fit
key_sources: Moll K., Snowling M. J., Göbel S. M., Hulme C. (2015). Early language and executive skills predict variations in number and arithmetic skills in children at family-risk of dyslexia and typically developing controls. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.03.004

article_title: Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design
citation: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y
title: The venue construct: a virtual collaboration space emerging from negotiated agreement on problems and objectives
description: From Alterman and Harsch's study of wiki- and blog-based collaborative writing, the editorial presents the "conceptual construct of a venue" as "a virtual space for collaboration that emerges as the participants succeed in negotiating an agreement on the problem(s) and objective(s) for joint problem solving." The nature of a venue depends on task design (e.g., role assignment) and the online platform; different venues afford different collaboration practices.
requirements: Participants must succeed in negotiating agreement on problems and objectives for joint problem solving for a venue to emerge
constraints: The venue's nature depends on task design and platform features; issues of ownership, identity and participation differ between wikis and blogs
target_learners: undergraduate students in small groups of five to seven
target_learning_goals: joint problem solving and collaborative writing in asynchronous online settings
examples: 19 teams in an undergraduate Internet and Society course completed four collaborative writing projects alternating between wiki-based and blog-based environments
key_sources: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y

article_title: Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy
citation: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y
title: Demonstrate an adequate false positive rate before adopting a measure of metacognitive accuracy
description: The article argues that researchers should not assume a measurement method controls its error rate; instead, each candidate measure of metacognitive accuracy should be shown via simulation or prior evidence to hold the false positive rate near the nominal alpha level. As the authors state, "we strongly recommend that only measures for which it has been demonstrated that the false positive rate is appropriate should be used." This applies to both summary-statistic and hierarchical approaches.
requirements: Simulation or empirical evidence that the measure's false positive rate is at or near the nominal alpha level for the intended design
constraints: The article notes the false-positive rate is only one consideration; validity and confounding by task performance and criteria must also be weighed
target_learners: Researchers studying metacognition in perceptual, memory, and cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of metacognitive accuracy in learning research
examples: The study itself evaluated gamma correlations, confidence slopes, type 2 ROCs, meta-d′, meta-da, HMeta-d, and logistic mixed regression via hierarchical resampling from the confidence database
key_sources: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y

article_title: How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning?
citation: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w
title: Vector quantization of group heart-rate data to detect group-level physiological state transitions
description: The study treats the collaborating group as a dynamic system whose aggregated state is a three-dimensional vector of the members' heart rates, traced over the exam session. Vector quantization (VQ) discretizes the continuously varying heart-rate triplets: "This technique allowed the reduction of the number of system states and transitions between them, giving rise to delineable recurrent state patterns." Transitions occur when the heart-rate triplet changes enough to associate with another centroid in the codebook, making state pattern analysis feasible and allowing alignment of physiological state transitions with regulatory sequences.
requirements: Heart-rate data collected from all group members simultaneously (Empatica S4 bracelets were used for three of the nine groups)
constraints: Physiological analysis was available for only three groups, due to limited bracelets
target_learners: high school students collaborating face-to-face during an exam task
target_learning_goals: detecting group-level regulatory processes and physiological state changes during collaborative learning
examples: Heart-rate triplets from three group members were represented as a trajectory in a three-dimensional coordinate system, then discretized into centroid-based states with transitions between them
key_sources: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w

article_title: Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review
citation: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001
title: Vermunt and Verloop's categorization of regulative and affective instructional strategies
description: The review adopts Vermunt and Verloop's (1999) framework of instructional activities that assist students in regulating their learning. For learning processes, "this framework distinguishes between four categories of regulative strategies: orienting and planning, monitoring, adjusting, and evaluating." For the affective climate, it distinguishes five categories of affective strategies: motivating, concentrating and exerting effort, attributing and judging oneself, appraising, and dealing with emotions. The review used these categories as the basis of its coding scheme and derived specific instructional activities (e.g. peer assessment, tracking learners, reminders) inductively within them.
requirements: The framework focuses on aspects that can be dealt with during instruction, making it suitable for analyzing course-level design
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of learning
affective climate in blended courses
examples: The review's coding scheme mapped activities such as measuring prior knowledge to orienting and planning, and online tests and tracking systems to monitoring
key_sources: Boelens, R., De Wever, B., & Voet, M. (2017). Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: A systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.06.001

article_title: A Complete SMOCkery: Daily Online Testing Did Not Boost College Performance
citation: Robinson, D. H. (2021). A Complete SMOCkery: Daily Online Testing Did Not Boost College Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09588-0
title: Vet widely cited educational claims for internal-validity threats before acting on them, and expose unsupported extravagant claims
description: The article demonstrates a practice of re-examining influential findings by checking threats to internal validity — history, selection bias, and differential attrition — before accepting causal claims from non-randomized comparisons. The author writes that "our field needs watchdogs who expose such unsupported extravagant claims— especially those appearing in pay-to-publish journals." The reanalysis of the SMOC data shows how alternative explanations can fully account for apparent effects.
requirements: Access to the underlying data or comparable institutional records, as the author accessed student major data for both cohorts
constraints: Applies to comparisons that do not randomly assign students to conditions; the author notes the original study was an ex post facto comparison of 2008 and 2011 cohorts
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of educational intervention evidence
examples: The author computed major-weighted average GPAs for the 2008 and 2011 introductory psychology cohorts and found the 0.11 weighted difference matched the originally reported advantages
key_sources: Robinson, D. H. (2021). A Complete SMOCkery: Daily Online Testing Did Not Boost College Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09588-0

article_title: A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Understanding Expert Scaffolding of Visual Problem-Solving Tasks: A Scoping Review
citation: Christine C. A. van Nooijen · Bjorn B. de Koning · Wichor M. Bramer · Anna Isahakyan · Maryam Asoodar · Ellen Kok · Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer · Fred Paas. (2024). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Understanding Expert Scaffolding of Visual Problem-Solving Tasks: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09848-3
title: A two-axis expression-and-activity taxonomy: scaffolding behaviours vary in verbal/nonverbal expression and active/passive engagement
description: Beyond cognitive strategy, the review codes scaffolding behaviours by method of expression (verbal/auditory vs. nonverbal/visual, which can co-occur, e.g. an expert narrating actions) and by an inductively derived activity category. The active/passive category, derived from Tambaum's concept of indirect scaffolding, captures purposeful absence: "the turns in which the tutor is available for the learner but only observes the learner acting independently and does not interfere even when the learner faces a problem". Passive excerpts were not further coded into expression or strategy categories because they describe the absence of behaviour.
requirements: Coding of excerpts requires isolating each expert-novice interaction event reported close to the original dataset
constraints: Passive excerpts cannot be sub-categorised as verbal/nonverbal or cueing/chunking because the category describes absence of behaviour
target_learners: Novices in visual domains taught in one-on-one apprenticeship-style settings
target_learning_goals: Visual expertise and visual problem-solving skill
examples: Of 164 included excerpts, 13 were coded passive; combined verbal-nonverbal expression occurred in 28 excerpts
key_sources: Christine C. A. van Nooijen · Bjorn B. de Koning · Wichor M. Bramer · Anna Isahakyan · Maryam Asoodar · Ellen Kok · Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer · Fred Paas. (2024). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Understanding Expert Scaffolding of Visual Problem-Solving Tasks: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09848-3

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Three-component taxonomy of learning activities: cognitive processing, affective, and metacognitive regulation
description: The article organizes student learning activities into three components drawn from Pintrich's comparison of taxonomies: cognitive processing, affective, and metacognitive (regulative) activities. Cognitive processing activities are "those thinking activities that students use to process subject matter and that lead directly to learning outcomes in terms of changes in students' knowledge base". Six processing categories (relating/structuring, analyzing, concretizing/applying, memorizing/rehearsing, critical processing, selecting), five affective categories, and five regulative categories (orienting/planning through evaluating/reflecting) are described, with the caveat that categories are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive.
requirements: Applies to upper secondary and higher education learning contexts as scoped by the article
constraints: The authors state the taxonomy is "not the ultimate solution but a helpful balance between simplified dichotomous categories and complex and elaborate categorical systems" and that categories are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive
target_learners: upper secondary and higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated knowledge construction across cognitive, affective and regulative learning activities
examples: Table 1 summarizes the categorization of learning activities across the three components
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Congruence and friction between learning and teaching
citation: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753
title: Four learning styles: undirected, reproduction-directed, meaning-directed and application-directed
description: The article defines learning style as a coherent whole of learning activities, learning orientation and conception of learning characteristic of a student in a certain period. Citing Vermunt's (1996, 1998) research, it reports "four qualitatively different learning styles as conceptualized above: undirected, reproduction-directed, meaning-directed and application-directed learning". Each style combines a processing strategy, a regulation strategy, a learning conception and an orientation; for example, the meaning-directed style combines deep processing, self-regulation, a knowledge-construction conception and personal interest.
requirements: Learning style is used broadly, including conceptions and orientations, not only consistent activity patterns
constraints: The article scopes this conceptualization to higher education students and notes family resemblances to Biggs's and Entwistle's orientations
target_learning_goals: diagnosing students' learning strategies and styles to tailor teaching
examples: The reproduction-directed style links stepwise processing and external regulation with a conception of learning as intake of teacher-provided knowledge
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt, Nico Verloop. (1999). Congruence and friction between learning and teaching. Learning and Instruction 9, 257–280. http://hdl.handle.net/1874/18753

article_title: Response practice as a factor in transfer of training
citation: Peterson, Lewis V. (1953). Use of Graphs in Air Force Teaching Materials. Division of Communications, University of Illinois, Human Resources Research Institute Research Memo #14, Maxwell AFB, Alabama, August 1953; with Eckstrand, Gordon A., Response Practice as a Factor in Transfer of Training, WADC Tech. Rpt. #6017. Research Abstracts, p. 157.
title: Vertical display panel apparatus for response-pretraining transfer research
description: Eckstrand's experiment used "A vertical display panel" through which "Any one of four colors or four letters could be exposed," with subjects pressing "the appropriate reaction key" when a color appeared. The apparatus embodies the design problem of simulating operator responses cheaply while the relevant stimuli are difficult and expensive to simulate in detail in training devices.
requirements: Requires a display panel with an aperture exposing color or letter stimuli and reaction keys for responses
constraints: Designed for tasks where simulating the stimuli in detail is difficult and expensive, so pretraining uses substitute letter stimuli
target_learners: Adult trainees (approximately 30 men per group in the experiment)
target_learning_goals: Transfer of trained manual responses to the actual task
examples: Pretraining trials used letters rather than colors as stimuli to which subjects pressed the reaction keys

article_title: Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development
citation: Rapanta, C., Maina, M., Lotz, N., & Bacchelli, A. (2013). Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development. Educational Technology Research and Development, 61(4), 581-605. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9306-5
title: Extended verbal protocol dataset of 15 e-learning design team meetings
description: The study's empirical corpus consists of video-recorded project meetings from two interdisciplinary e-learning course teams at well-established European distance universities. "In total, 15 project meetings (10 from Team A and 5 from Team B) were video-recorded and 25.7 meeting hours were totally transcribed." Team A was observed for one year during a 60-credit Bachelor course on Design Thinking; Team B for half a year during a 6-credit Masters course on Instructional Design Models. Meetings were situated in the development phase of design.
requirements: Meetings were situated in the development phase, after course structure and objectives had been decided
constraints: Only interaction moments with reflective decision-making formed the final dataset, segmented into topic-based episodes, sequences, and moves
target_learners: interdisciplinary e-learning design team members in higher education
target_learning_goals: describing and improving team instructional design processes
examples: Team A won a quality award for its course, supporting the teams' representativeness of high-quality design
key_sources: Rapanta, C., Maina, M., Lotz, N., & Bacchelli, A. (2013). Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development. Educational Technology Research and Development, 61(4), 581-605. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9306-5

article_title: Seeking the Optimal Time for Integrated Curriculum in Jinan University School of Medicine
citation: Sanqiang Pan, Xin Cheng, Yanghai Zhou, Ke Li & Xuesong Yang. (2017). Seeking the Optimal Time for Integrated Curriculum in Jinan University School of Medicine. International Journal of Higher Education, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v6n1p25
title: Schedule vertical integrated curriculum after students have mastered basic sciences, around year 3
description: The article recommends beginning vertical integrated curriculum in year 3, once students have completed basic medical sciences, rather than in year 1. It concludes that "year 3 is the optimal timing taking integrated course, after students have mastered quite basic science knowledge," based on its exam, questionnaire and OSCE comparisons between year 1 and year 3 participants.
requirements: Students should have completed core basic medical sciences (physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, microbiology, immunology, pathology/pathophysiology) before entering integrated courses
constraints: Conclusion drawn from a single school's elective summer courses with volunteer participants scoring at or above Grade B; the authors note precise analysis on each specialization should be further completed later on
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and analytical thinking about clinical diseases
integration of basic science knowledge with clinical medicine
examples: Jinan University School of Medicine offered 45-hour elective integrated courses on cardiovascular and respiratory systems using lectures, demonstration, intern rotations and PBL, taught by trained faculty from basic and clinical sciences
key_sources: Sanqiang Pan, Xin Cheng, Yanghai Zhou, Ke Li & Xuesong Yang. (2017). Seeking the Optimal Time for Integrated Curriculum in Jinan University School of Medicine. International Journal of Higher Education, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v6n1p25

article_title: Supporting Student Veterans: Utilizing Game-Based Role-Plays with Virtual Humans to Build Military Cultural Competency and Helping Behaviors in Faculty and Staff
citation: Cate, C. A., & Albright, G. (2015). Supporting Student Veterans: Utilizing Game-Based Role-Plays with Virtual Humans to Build Military Cultural Competency and Helping Behaviors in Faculty and Staff. Online Learning, 19(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1074245
title: Veterans on Campus (VOC): a 30-minute online game-based role-play simulation with emotionally responsive virtual student veterans.
description: VOC is "a 30-minute online training simulation designed to educate faculty and staff" about the unique value student veterans bring to campus, obstacles veterans face, techniques for managing veteran-sensitive classroom discussions, and best practices for connecting distressed student veterans with support services. It is "built around a series of mini-conversation games where users interact with intelligent, fully animated, and emotionally responsive virtual student veterans." A virtual coach provides ongoing positive and corrective feedback as learners practice motivational interviewing skills. VOC was developed by Kognito with input from veteran services organizations, mental health experts, and over 75 faculty and student veterans, and is listed in Section III of the Suicide Prevention Resource Center Best Practices Registry.
requirements: Users must complete role-plays with three emotionally responsive virtual student veterans, receiving feedback from a virtual coach, to finish the training.
target_learning_goals: understand the value and challenges of student veterans
manage veteran-sensitive classroom discussions
connect distressed student veterans with support services
key_sources: Cate, C. A., & Albright, G. (2015). Supporting Student Veterans: Utilizing Game-Based Role-Plays with Virtual Humans to Build Military Cultural Competency and Helping Behaviors in Faculty and Staff. Online Learning, 19(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061484

article_title: Evaluating the Impact of Computer-Based and Traditional Learning Environments on Students' Knowledge of Algebra
citation: Krupa, E., Webel, C., & McManus, J. (2013). Evaluating the impact of computer-based and traditional learning environments on students' knowledge of algebra. In Martinez, M. & Castro Superfine, A (Eds.), Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. Chicago, IL: University of Illinois at Chicago.
title: Verify that cost-effective delivery methods promote conceptual understanding, not only procedural fluency
description: When universities adopt cost-effective technology-mediated instruction, institutions should verify these methods are effective "not only in promoting students' procedural fluency but also in providing students with a rich experience that shows them the connections behind algorithmic procedures." This study suggests emporium students may gain procedural fluency yet be "limited in their ability to interpret mathematical objects and relate them to contextual situations." Assessment should therefore include non-routine tasks requiring interpretation and justification, not only procedural exams.
requirements: Assessment instruments must include non-routine problem-solving tasks that ask students to interpret equations in context and justify conclusions
constraints: Based on a single quasi-experimental study at one mid-sized suburban university; the authors note more work is needed given the limited number of empirical studies on emporium-style courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of algebraic functions in context
procedural fluency
examples: The study gave students four problem-solving items near the end of the semester, including a ticket-price revenue task asking whether increasing price always increases income
key_sources: Krupa, E., Webel, C., & McManus, J. (2013). Evaluating the impact of computer-based and traditional learning environments on students' knowledge of algebra. In Martinez, M. & Castro Superfine, A (Eds.), Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. Chicago, IL: University of Illinois at Chicago. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED584492

(2014). Journal of Prevention & Intervention in the Community, 42:3, 221-242. https://doi.org/10.1080/10852352.2014.916586
title: Vet developing interventions with community stakeholders and incorporate their feedback into design decisions.
description: The article's fourth development step was to "identify components that are essential for stakeholder (i.e., school administrators, teachers, parents, students) investment in our intervention and to ensure the intervention is culturally and contextually relevant to those stakeholders". Nine focus groups and 12 community advisory board meetings were held, and stakeholder input produced two concrete design changes: shifting the target grade from 8th to 6th and shifting from a short-term to a long-term commitment model.
requirements: Partnerships with schools and community organization leaders
Focus groups and community advisory board meetings to gather feedback
constraints: Stakeholder feedback is specific to the community context; the article notes other elements developed from research with this population were deemed culturally and contextually relevant
target_learning_goals: academic engagement
school completion
examples: Nine focus groups (two with male students; two with female students; three with parents; and two with teachers and school staff members) and 12 community advisory board meetings were conducted in the Englewood community of Chicago.

article_title: Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study.
citation: Shin Sujin, Choi Jaehwa, Hong Eunmin, Lee Miji, Go Jinseon, Yu Subin, Lee Minjae. (2026). Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09685-8
title: VEGA: a generative AI agent that automatically generates NCJMM-aligned vignette-based item sets with immediate feedback
description: VEGA is a generative AI agent, built on the Collective AI on the Foundation AI (CAFA) platform using GPT-4.1-nano via the OpenAI API, that "automatically generates vignette-based item sets, defined as short clinical scenarios followed by structured assessment items." Learners select a body system, receive a vignette with six NCJMM-aligned items, submit responses through a chat interface, and receive immediate feedback with explanatory rationales. Development followed the ADDIE model with few-shot prompting from NCSBN exemplar items.
requirements: Requires a GPT Application Programming Interface (API) key provided by the user
constraints: The article states the quality of AI-generated outputs, including clinical accuracy and psychometric properties, could not be systematically verified because VEGA continuously generates new items rather than administering a fixed item set
target_learners: third- and fourth-year undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: clinical judgment and clinical reasoning across six NCJMM stages
examples: In the pilot, 12 students used VEGA freely for one week, completing a minimum of six item sets with screenshots uploaded for fidelity monitoring
key_sources: Shin Sujin, Choi Jaehwa, Hong Eunmin, Lee Miji, Go Jinseon, Yu Subin, Lee Minjae. (2026). Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09685-8

article_title: Impact of a vertically integrated, symptom-oriented teaching program for hematuria management on clinical competency transfer among urology clerkship students.
citation: Peng Shuang, Wei Yongbao, Dai Caixia, Liang Yuxuan, Huang Li. (2026). Impact of a vertically integrated, symptom-oriented teaching program for hematuria management on clinical competency transfer among urology clerkship students. BMC Medical Education, 26, Article 1348. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09680-z
title: Vertically integrated hematuria management teaching program (modular teaching + formative assessment + feedback loop)
description: A symptom-oriented, pathway-based clerkship teaching program that constructs a repeatable diagnostic and management pathway with hematuria as the main thread. Its core idea was to encourage closed-loop competence from symptom to decision through modular training, and constantly correct learning deviations by means of formative assessment and feedback in real time. Four consecutive weekly modules covered risk stratification, test strategy and interpretation, safe management/referral decisions, and structured case presentation with modified OSCE evaluation, supported by checklists and decision cards.
requirements: Same senior teacher uniformly designed and led key components across cohorts to ensure implementation consistency
constraints: Delivered by a single senior teacher, so pathway-design benefits cannot be separated from teacher expertise and enthusiasm
Single-center, single-theme module with follow-up only to the end of rotation
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning and risk stratification in hematuria management
Safe management and referral decisions in high-risk scenarios
Risk communication and follow-up planning
examples: Weeks 1–3 focused on risk stratification, test strategy and results interpretation, and safe management/referral decisions with weekly tests and centralized feedback; week 4 included structured case presentation and the modified OSCE.
key_sources: Peng Shuang, Wei Yongbao, Dai Caixia, Liang Yuxuan, Huang Li. (2026). Impact of a vertically integrated, symptom-oriented teaching program for hematuria management on clinical competency transfer among urology clerkship students. BMC Medical Education, 26, Article 1348. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09680-z

article_title: Ophthalmic surgical simulator: an effective and safe approach for trainees in vitreoretinal surgery.
citation: Giannuzzi Federico, Hu Lorenzo, Carlà Matteo Mario, Cestrone Valentina, Marcelli Sofia, De Vico Umberto, Savastano Alfonso, Crincoli Emanuele, Savastano Maria Cristina, Rizzo Stanislao. (2025). Ophthalmic surgical simulator: an effective and safe approach for trainees in vitreoretinal surgery. International Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10792-025-03851-5
title: Vergence-accommodation conflict as a mechanism for transient stereopsis reduction in VR simulator use
description: The article invokes the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC) to explain the transient stereopsis reduction observed after EyeSi use. The EyeSi "presents disparity cues that stimulate vergence, while the accommodative demand remains fixed at the optical plane of the display", requiring eyes to converge to perceive virtual depth while accommodation stays fixed at the display's focal plane. The authors suggest this mismatch produces transient visual fatigue, consistent with prior reports that healthy individuals with normal baseline stereopsis show no improvement or transient worsening after VR exposure.
requirements: A stereoscopic display presenting disparity cues that stimulate vergence while accommodative demand remains fixed
constraints: The effect described applies to individuals with normal baseline stereopsis; VR-based orthoptic training has improved stereoacuity in individuals with pre-existing binocular vision deficits
target_learners: ophthalmology trainees using VR surgical simulators
target_learning_goals: understanding unintended visual effects of VR simulator use on stereopsis and binocular vision
examples: The authors attribute the shift toward higher TNO stereoacuity values in their cohort to transient visual fatigue due to the demands of the VR environment and the VAC
key_sources: Giannuzzi Federico, Hu Lorenzo, Carlà Matteo Mario, Cestrone Valentina, Marcelli Sofia, De Vico Umberto, Savastano Alfonso, Crincoli Emanuele, Savastano Maria Cristina, Rizzo Stanislao. (2025). Ophthalmic surgical simulator: an effective and safe approach for trainees in vitreoretinal surgery. International Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10792-025-03851-5

article_title: Training the trainees in robotic surgery - a pilot scheme in the United Kingdom.
citation: Al-Ani Mohammed, Massias Samuel, Jayawardena Panduka, Khanderia Esha, Franklyn Joshua, Hashmi Khawar, Patel Vanash. (2025). Training the trainees in robotic surgery – a pilot scheme in the United Kingdom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07749-9
title: Versius Trainer proficiency-based simulation with expert-benchmarked performance metrics
description: The Versius Trainer is the virtual simulation component of the pilot pathway, consisting of 16 proficiency-based tasks such as instrument navigation, endoscope control, peg transfer and running suturing. Each task has "measurable metrics such as the combined instrument tip path length to reaching the object, combined instrument angular path and combined instruments out of view", and performance scores are "compared with benchmarks set to the average performance of experts completing the training tasks". Trainees' attempts per task were tracked and analysed in the pilot evaluation.
requirements: Trainees must meet the task-specific proficiency benchmarks, with starred tasks passed two times consecutively and three times in total
constraints: Benchmarks and tasks are specific to the CMR Surgical Versius platform
target_learners: General surgical specialist trainees learning robotic console skills
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor robotic console skills including instrument navigation, camera control, dissection, suturing and knot-tying
examples: Tasks marked with * in the article's Table 2 must be passed 2 times consecutively and 3 times in total; all other tasks must be passed once
key_sources: Al-Ani Mohammed, Massias Samuel, Jayawardena Panduka, Khanderia Esha, Franklyn Joshua, Hashmi Khawar, Patel Vanash. (2025). Training the trainees in robotic surgery – a pilot scheme in the United Kingdom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07749-9

article_title: Essential Newborn Care Virtual Simulations for Skills Retention in Newborn Care.
citation: Umoren RA, Ezeaka C, Berkelhamer SK, et al. (2025). Essential Newborn Care Virtual Simulations for Skills Retention in Newborn Care. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.60565
title: Virtual Essential Newborn Care (vENC) mobile virtual simulation app
description: The vENC app is a mobile virtual simulation for smartphones or tablets in which health professionals "use their eyes or hands to interact with a 3-dimensional or virtual reality (VR) experience" to practice essential newborn care. Each simulation begins with preparation for the birth and covers skin-to-skin care, weight and temperature, eye and cord care, and vitamin K, with acuity classification as green, yellow, or red. Learners receive "step-by-step guidance, automated feedback, and a final score" based on approximately 100 within-scenario actions. The app is small enough to download on slow connections and works offline, syncing to a DHIS2 database when connected.
requirements: A smartphone or tablet capable of running the app; a study phone with a low-cost VR headset was used in this study
Internet connection only needed to sync usage data to the online database
constraints: Not all phones can run virtual simulations; some participants reported slow navigation on older devices and nausea or headache in VR mode
target_learners: nurses and midwives providing newborn care in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: essential newborn care skills including neonatal resuscitation, skin-to-skin care, and newborn assessment
examples: Used at variable recommended frequencies (2-12 scenarios per month) by 70 nurses and midwives in Lagos for 6 months after in-person ENC training
key_sources: Umoren RA, Ezeaka C, Berkelhamer SK, et al. (2025). Essential Newborn Care Virtual Simulations for Skills Retention in Newborn Care. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.60565

article_title: Simulation training with haptic feedback of instrument vibrations reduces resident workload during live robot-assisted sleeve gastrectomy.
citation: Gomez ED, Husin HM, Dumon KR, Williams NN, Kuchenbecker KJ. (2024). Simulation training with haptic feedback of instrument vibrations reduces resident workload during live robot-assisted sleeve gastrectomy. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11459-6
title: VerroTouch naturalistic vibrotactile haptic feedback system for da Vinci robotic instruments
description: VerroTouch is a haptic feedback system that "uses low-cost sensors and actuators to allow the surgeon to feel the vibrations of the left and right da Vinci instruments at their fingertips", vibrations caused by transient physical events such as sudden contact with a stiff object or releases of tension. In this study it delivered naturalistic vibrotactile feedback through the da Vinci handles during the first four of five simulated bariatric procedures for the haptic group. Prior user studies cited found it did not interfere with teleoperation and positively affected perceived concentration ability.
requirements: Requires sensors and actuators mounted on the da Vinci instruments to detect and present instrument vibration transients through the console handles.
constraints: Feedback was delivered only in simulation; live procedures in this study were performed without haptic feedback, and the authors note feeling mechanical vibrations is only one modality of the sense of touch.
target_learners: General surgery residents (PGY-3 and PGY-7) learning robotic surgery
target_learning_goals: Robotic surgical skill acquisition with reduced cognitive workload
examples: In this study, the haptic group received VerroTouch feedback during the first four of five simulated bariatric surgeries on a custom inanimate simulator.
key_sources: Gomez ED, Husin HM, Dumon KR, Williams NN, Kuchenbecker KJ. (2024). Simulation training with haptic feedback of instrument vibrations reduces resident workload during live robot-assisted sleeve gastrectomy. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11459-6

article_title: Effect of E-learning clinical management of substance-dependent pregnant women on the knowledge and clinical skill performance of midwives: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Heidarian H, Mehrabi M, Ghaemmaghami P, Janghorban R. (2025). Effect of E-learning clinical management of substance-dependent pregnant women on the knowledge and clinical skill performance of midwives: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-024-07130-6
title: Vesta LMS e-learning program: ten sessions on clinical management of substance-dependent pregnant women
description: The intervention is a four-week e-learning program delivered through Vesta, a learning management system belonging to Shiraz University of Medical Sciences. Content covers "the effects of six types of substances" and labor, postpartum, breastfeeding, and neonatal abstinence syndrome care across ten sessions in Persian, generated under content production standards and nine implementation stages, with pictures, diagrams, clinical videos, patient scenarios, and quizzes. Sessions were released every three days, and gated self-assessment tests of 3–6 questions had to be passed (with two permitted attempts) to progress.
requirements: Access to a computer and internet and minimum computer skills to enter the LMS
Passing each session's self-assessment test to participate in the next session
constraints: Evaluated for midwives in governmental maternity hospitals with 4 weeks of training and a one-month follow-up
target_learners: Working midwives in governmental maternity hospitals
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and clinical skill performance in caring for substance-dependent pregnant women during labor and post-partum
examples: Midwives accessed content at any hour of the day and night by logging into the LMS through a computer, with one session provided every three days over four weeks
key_sources: Heidarian H, Mehrabi M, Ghaemmaghami P, Janghorban R. (2025). Effect of E-learning clinical management of substance-dependent pregnant women on the knowledge and clinical skill performance of midwives: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-024-07130-6

article_title: Training and assessing undergraduate medical students' research: Learning, engagement and experiences of students and staff.
citation: Mahomed S, Ross A, Van Wyk J. (2021). Training and assessing undergraduate medical students’ research: Learning, engagement and experiences of students and staff. Afr J Prm Health Care Fam Med. https://doi.org/10.4102/phcfm.v13i1.2559
title: Longitudinal, vertically aligned research modules embedded across three years of an undergraduate medical programme
description: The Selective 01–03 modules form a compulsory, community-orientated research strand running through years two to four of the 6-year MBChB programme. The article states these modules are "incremental and vertically aligned to develop students’ research competence longitudinally over a 3-year period". Each year builds on the previous: topic selection and literature review, then protocol, ethics approval, data collection and poster presentation, then an intervention. All students participate rather than a self-selected few.
requirements: All students complete each stage in sequence, with supervisor allocation, ethics committee review, and a structured marking rubric for the poster assessment
constraints: Described and evaluated in a single cohort at one South African medical school; the authors note limited generalisability because of the unique context
target_learning_goals: research methodology competence, evidence-based medicine, community-orientated primary care
examples: In 2018, 250 third-year students in 86 groups of two to five wrote protocols, obtained ethical approval, collected data, and presented posters at an annual research day with 10-minute presentations and 5-minute question sessions
key_sources: Mahomed S, Ross A, Van Wyk J. (2021). Training and assessing undergraduate medical students’ research: Learning, engagement and experiences of students and staff. Afr J Prm Health Care Fam Med. https://doi.org/10.4102/phcfm.v13i1.2559

article_title: Developing a video-based method to compare and adjust examiner effects in fully nested OSCEs.
citation: Yeates P, Cope N, Hawarden A, Bradshaw H, McCray G, Homer M. (2019). Developing a video‐based method to compare and adjust examiner effects in fully nested OSCEs. Medical Education, 53(3), 250–263. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13783
title: VESCA: video-based examiner score comparison and adjustment for fully nested OSCEs
description: VESCA is a three-phase method for measuring and adjusting examiner-cohort effects in fully nested, multi-circuit OSCEs. It involves "(i) a subset of students were filmed ‘live’ when performing the majority of stations in their real OSCE; (ii) examiners from each of the separate parallel circuits of the examination scored station‐specific common‐comparator videos", and (iii) statistical analysis (MFRM for global scores, LMM for percentage scores) uses the partial crossing to estimate and adjust cohort effects. The article presents it as novel because scoring station-specific common-comparator videos overcomes the fully nested design without assuming equal student ability across cohorts.
requirements: Volunteer students must be filmed on most stations with consent; examiners from every cohort must score the station-specific common-comparator videos to create partial crossing between cohorts
Statistical analysis (MFRM and LMM) must model student, station and examiner-cohort facets concurrently to control for both examiner bias and student ability
constraints: VESCA "would neither measure nor adjust" other systematic differences between circuits such as simulated-patient difficulty
It treats cohort stringency as fixed effects, ignoring examiner × student interactions and rater idiosyncrasy, and does not model rater drift or contrast effects
Dependability of linkage with only two videos per examiner (up to 20 per cohort) is unclear, especially for cohorts with lower participation rates
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in high-stakes summative OSCEs
target_learning_goals: Fair and equivalent summative assessment of clinical skills across parallel circuits or geographical sites
examples: In the pilot, five volunteers were filmed on 10 of 12 stations of a four-lane Year-3 OSCE; 49 of 67 examiners (73.1%) scored comparator videos, and cohort estimates were based on 10–20 comparator videos per cohort
key_sources: Yeates P, Cope N, Hawarden A, Bradshaw H, McCray G, Homer M. (2019). Developing a video‐based method to compare and adjust examiner effects in fully nested OSCEs. Medical Education, 53(3), 250–263. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13783

article_title: Predictors of confidence in anatomy knowledge for work as a junior doctor: a national survey of Australian medical students.
citation: Farey John E., Bui David T., Townsend David, Sureshkumar Premala, Carr Sandra, Roberts Chris. (2018). Predictors of confidence in anatomy knowledge for work as a junior doctor: a national survey of Australian medical students. BMC Medical Education 18:174. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1280-5
title: Design anatomy curricula that vertically integrate teaching and consistent regular assessment across pre-clinical and clinical stages and integrate anatomy with other basic sciences
description: The article recommends that medical educators enhance student confidence by developing curricula that "vertically integrat[e] anatomy learning and teaching", integrate anatomy with other basic sciences, and provide "consistent assessment through both the pre-clinical and clinical stages". These are the modifiable factors the survey's regression identified as positively associated with confidence. The recommendation rests on cross-sectional self-report data, not on tested curriculum interventions.
requirements: Anatomy teaching must continue into the clinical years, not only the pre-clinical curriculum
constraints: Self-reported confidence does not equate to competence, as the authors acknowledge
target_learning_goals: anatomy knowledge sufficient for practice as a junior doctor
examples: The survey found 57.5% of respondents reported too little integration of anatomy with clinical teaching and 54.7% reported too little anatomy assessment.
key_sources: Farey John E., Bui David T., Townsend David, Sureshkumar Premala, Carr Sandra, Roberts Chris. (2018). Predictors of confidence in anatomy knowledge for work as a junior doctor: a national survey of Australian medical students. BMC Medical Education 18:174. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1280-5

article_title: General practitioners as educators in adolescent health: a training evaluation.
citation: Van de Mortel T, Bird J, Chown P, Trigger R, Ahern C. (2016). General practitioners as educators in adolescent health: a training evaluation. BMC Family Practice 17:32. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-016-0432-0
title: Vertically integrated teaching teams pairing GPs, registrars and medical students to co-facilitate school health education
description: The intervention took a vertically integrated (VI) approach, forming teaching teams of one GP, one registrar and one medical student, or one GP with one or two medical students, which then co-facilitated 90-minute health education sessions at secondary schools. The rationale is that registrars and students, being closer in age to school students, "may be seen as more approachable by adolescents, which can help to create a bridge between older GPs and adolescents", while GPs bring greater knowledge of adolescent health issues. The authors suggest this mix "may offer a model for building confidence and skills across the medical education continuum."
requirements: Teams must include members at multiple levels of the medical education continuum
Teams must be large enough to deliver sessions to six or seven small groups at each secondary school
constraints: Small sample sizes made comparative analysis between participant levels invalid in this evaluation
target_learning_goals: Delivering community-based adolescent health education
Small group facilitation and co-facilitation skills
examples: Each team co-facilitated 90-minute health education sessions with Year 11 students (aged ~16–17) at one to two high schools in their area
